name: Title
low: Clickbait: Uses hype such as 'miracle', 'proves', 'cure', 'shocking' or 'breakthrough', or promises far more than the study shows.
medium: Modest: Calmly worded, but slightly overstates the finding or leaves out an important limit, such as who was studied or that it shows only a link.
high: Accurate: Boring but true. Says what was studied, in whom and what was found, with any key limit (for example 'Coffee linked to shorter sleep in mice').

name: Access
low: Closed: Almost no one can read it. The full paper costs money (often £30 or more) with no free copy, or only a summary is public.
medium: Restricted: Only some people can read it free. Readers need a university login or a sign-up, or must ask for a copy or know where to find one.
high: Open: Anyone can read the full paper or report free online, with no login or sign-up (open access).

name: Source
low: Suspicious: Predatory journals (pay to publish, no real peer review), blogs, websites, videos or magazines with no outside checks. Also reports by companies or interest groups on their own products (white papers).
medium: Use with caution: Preprints (not yet peer reviewed) and average or less selective journals, or ones keen on eye-catching results. Also peer-reviewed work paid for or checked by people with a stake in the result.
high: Trusted: Selective or well-established peer-reviewed journals (such as those of large scientific societies), independent research bodies or government agencies. No funder has a stake in the result.

name: Theory
low: Unfounded: Ignores or goes against well-established science, or rests on an idea with no evidence behind it.
medium: Sound but limited: Builds reasonably on accepted research, but has a weak point. It rests on an untested assumption, skips other explanations or fills no clear gap.
high: Robust: Uses past research responsibly to fill a clear gap in knowledge. Examples are a new question or a needed replication (repeating a study whose result is still uncertain).

name: Methods & Data
low: Flawed & Closed: No real study, a tiny sample, hand-picked evidence or a measure that cannot answer the question. No fair comparison (no control group, or groups that differ in obvious ways). The data are kept secret.
medium: Acceptable: A reasonable design and sample, but with clear weak points, for example no blinding, a one-off survey or people rating themselves. Data are partly shared or available on request.
high: Rigorous & Open: A strong design and a large enough sample for the question, for example groups chosen by chance, blinding, a preregistered plan and independent checks. Data are open, or shared through a set process that protects privacy.

name: Conclusion
low: Overblown: Claims far more than the evidence shows. It may treat a link as proof of cause or claim effects that were never measured.
medium: Logical: Mostly fits the evidence, but plays down limits or leaves out other explanations.
high: Nuanced: Careful. Claims only what the evidence shows and says plainly what the study cannot show.
